segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, even if a person is caught in some offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness—each of you watching yourself, so that you too are not tempted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if anyone thinks they are something when they are nothing, they are deluding themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But let each person examine their own work, and then they will have their reason to boast in themselves alone and not in someone else,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for each person will carry their own load.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who is instructed in the word should share all good things with the one who instructs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that they will also reap,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because the one who sows to their own flesh will reap decay from the flesh, but the one who sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let us not grow weary of doing what is right, for at the proper time we will reap, if we do not give up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, while we have time, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who belong to the household of the faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: See what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who want to make a good showing in the flesh are the ones trying to compel you to be circumcised—only so that they will not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For not even those who are circumcised keep the law themselves; they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as for me, may I never boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything; what matters is a new creation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as for all who will keep in step with this rule—peace be upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From now on, let no one cause me trouble, for I carry the marks of Jesus on my body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers and sisters. Amen.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to whole congregations. Older versions have “brethren” or “brothers”; many recent translations now render it “brothers and sisters” for the same reason.

The verb can mean that the person is detected by others in the act, or that the person is overtaken by the offense, caught off guard by it. “Caught in” leaves both possibilities open. Commentators are divided, though the gentle tone of the verse fits the idea of someone taken by surprise.

The word means a wrongful act, a moral failure. “Trespass” is the traditional rendering, but in current English it mainly suggests entering property without permission. English versions vary among “trespass”, “transgression”, “sin” and “offense”; the meaning itself is not disputed.

Older versions have “a spirit of meekness”. “Meek” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not; it describes a gentle, unassertive way of dealing with others. “Gentleness” is the usual rendering in modern translations.

Paul uses a different word here from the “burdens” of verse 2, and the translation keeps them distinct. Verse 2 concerns weights that others can help carry. This verse, following the call to self-examination, concerns the responsibility each person has for their own work, most likely with God’s final assessment in view. Older versions use “burden” in both places, which makes the two statements seem to conflict.

The verb is the ordinary one for sharing or partnership, and Paul uses related language elsewhere for financial support. Most interpreters take the verse as an instruction that those who receive teaching should support their teachers materially. “All good things” may be broader than money.

The word means decay, ruin or destruction, the rotting of what perishes, and here it stands as the opposite of eternal life. “Corruption” is the traditional rendering, but in modern English it chiefly suggests dishonesty or bribery. Some versions have “destruction”.

notes.traditional: how large a letter / what large letters
notes.note: Letters were normally dictated to a secretary, and the sender often added a closing in his own handwriting to authenticate it. Paul appears to take the pen at this point, though some think the remark covers the whole letter. Why his writing was large is unknown: emphasis, an unpracticed hand and poor eyesight have all been suggested. The King James “how large a letter” (a long epistle) is not what the Greek says.

The Greek is a present participle, which could mean “those who are circumcised” as a class (the people pressing for circumcision) or “those who are getting themselves circumcised” (converts who accept the rite). Some manuscripts read a perfect participle, “those who have been circumcised”. Most interpreters take it as a reference to the advocates of circumcision themselves.

The Greek pronoun can refer either to the cross (“through which”) or to Jesus Christ (“through whom”). Most modern translations choose the cross, since it is the object of the boasting and the next clause speaks of crucifixion. The King James has “by whom”. The sense differs little either way.

notes.phrase: and upon the Israel of God
notes.traditional: and upon the Israel of God
notes.note: This phrase is among the most disputed in the letter. The “and” may be explanatory (“that is, the Israel of God”), identifying all who follow this rule, Jew and Gentile alike, as God’s Israel. Or it may add a distinct group: Jewish believers, or the Jewish people for whom Paul wishes mercy. The translation keeps the Greek word order and the plain “and” so that both readings remain open.

notes.traditional: marks of the Lord Jesus / marks of Jesus
notes.note: The word was used for marks tattooed or branded on the body, especially those that identified a slave’s owner or a devotee’s god. Paul most likely means the scars left by beatings and stonings suffered in his work, which show whose servant he is. The later use of “stigmata” for wounds corresponding to those of the crucifixion is not in view.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs throughout the letters, and versions split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters”; it should not vary from chapter to chapter.

Paul’s ethical use (“sow to the flesh”) and his physical use (circumcision “in the flesh”) interlock here and across Romans and Galatians, and translators differ widely between “flesh”, “sinful nature” and others.
Whether to capitalize and how to render references to the Mosaic law versus law as a principle (“the law of Christ”) needs a single policy across Paul’s letters.
The verb and its nouns recur throughout Paul with both positive and negative force, and versions vary among “boast”, “glory”, “take pride” and “rejoice”.
It overlaps with πειράζω (“test” in the register) and recurs across the letters as “test”, “examine”, “prove” and “approve”, so the pair needs coordinated renderings.
